findings.title: Accidental git submodule added, pointing back at the PR's own base commit
findings.body: This PR adds a new file `sentry-repo` with mode/content indicating a git submodule pinned to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`, which is exactly the base commit of this same PR. This looks like an accidental artifact (e.g. from a bad `git submodule add` or tooling mistake) rather than an intentional change, has no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry shown, and is unrelated to the stated feature. Merging it risks broken clones/checkouts, confusing repo tooling, and bloats the diff with no functional purpose. It should be removed before merge.

findings.title: Upsampling eligibility check uses the outer closure `dataset` instead of the function's own `scoped_dataset` parameter
findings.body: Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, ...)`, the call `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` passes `dataset` — the module-level variable computed once in `get()` — instead of the function parameter `scoped_dataset`, which represents the actual dataset being queried for this specific call. In the dashboard-widget-split code path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked multiple times with different `scoped_dataset` values (e.g. `discover` for `errors_only_query`/`transactions_only_query`, or the original `scoped_dataset` for the main query) while the outer `dataset` stays fixed. As a result, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` evaluates against the wrong dataset module for these sub-calls, causing upsampling to be incorrectly enabled or disabled depending on which dataset was resolved at the top of `get()`, producing inconsistent/incorrect counts for dashboard widgets using the discover-split logic.

findings.title: `_is_error_focused_query` inspects the raw request query string, not the effective query used for the specific sub-call
findings.body: `_is_error_focused_query` (used by `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` for the discover dataset) always reads `request.GET.get("query", "")`, i.e. the original top-level request query. However, `_get_event_stats` is called with different, dynamically-constructed `query` strings in the dashboard-widget split flow (e.g. `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"`, `transactions_only_query`). The eligibility check never looks at these per-call query strings, so it can make the wrong upsampling decision (e.g. deciding not to upsample an errors-only sub-query because the raw request query didn't literally contain `event.type:error`, or vice versa).

findings.title: New `upsampled_count()` SnQL function is not marked `private`, bypassing the allowlist gating entirely
findings.body: The newly added `upsampled_count` `SnQLFunction` omits `private=True`, unlike the function immediately preceding it in the same list which does set `private=True`. Because it is registered in `function_converter`'s public function map without the private flag, any caller can directly request `upsampled_count()` via the public events/events-stats API (e.g. as `yAxis=upsampled_count()` or in `field`), for any project — not just those in `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. This completely bypasses the allowlist/eligibility checks implemented in `error_upsampling.py`, which were supposed to be the only gate controlling access to `sum(sample_weight)`-based counts.

findings.title: Cache key derived from Python's built-in `hash()` risks collisions across unrelated project sets
findings.body: `cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` uses the built-in `hash()` to fold the sorted project id tuple into the cache key. Distinct sets of project ids can map to the same hash value (hash collisions), which would cause the eligibility decision computed for one set of projects to be served from cache for a different, unrelated set of projects sharing the same organization id, within the 60s TTL. A deterministic, collision-resistant encoding (e.g. a delimited string of sorted ids) should be used instead of relying on `hash()`, which is also not part of any stable contract for this purpose.

findings.title: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is unused dead code — no mechanism actually invalidates the 60s eligibility cache
findings.body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to clear the cached allowlist-eligibility decision "when the allowlist configuration changes," but nothing in this diff calls it (no options-change hook, signal, or admin action wiring it up). Combined with the 60-second cache TTL in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, this means allowlist changes can silently take up to 60 seconds to propagate with no active invalidation path, and the presence of this function creates a false impression that cache consistency is actively managed.

findings.title: Bare `except Exception: pass` silently swallows all errors when deriving `sample_rate` from event contexts
findings.body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the dict traversal (`normalized_data.get("contexts", {}).get("error_sampling", {}).get("client_sample_rate")`) and the `float()` conversion in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks. If `contexts` is explicitly `None` (a valid value some code paths may set), `.get(...)` on `None` raises `AttributeError`, which is silently discarded. This means malformed or unexpected test fixture data will silently fail to populate `sample_rate` with no error or warning, making it hard to diagnose test failures or regressions that rely on this helper (used directly by `store_event`, a widely used test utility).

findings.title: No tests exercise the caching behavior of `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`
findings.body: The PR title advertises "performance optimizations" via caching, implemented in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss paths, 60s TTL) and `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. None of these are covered: the unit tests only exercise `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` directly, bypassing the caching wrapper entirely. There is no test verifying that a cached `True`/`False` eligibility value is actually reused on a subsequent call, that it expires correctly, or that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` has any effect.

findings.title: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact literal `count()`, missing aliased or spaced variants
findings.body: The transform does `if column_lower == "count()":` after lowercasing and stripping, so it only matches an exact `count()` token. Common query shapes like `count() as my_count`, `count(id)`, or any alias form will not be transformed, silently falling back to the regular (non-upsampled) count for those columns while other `count()` columns in the same request get upsampled. This produces inconsistent upsampling behavior across a single request/query without any error or indication to the caller.
